TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
WEDNESDAY, 01 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 3, DAY 3
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC, COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH MATT SHERMAN AND
CHRISTOPHER BESHARA, COUNSEL ASSISTING
PERRY HERZFELD SC, BORA KAPLAN SC, SOPHIE COULSON,
CHARLIE TAYLOR COUNSEL FOR THE COMMONWEALTH OF
AUSTRALIA
NAOMI SHARP SC, COUNSEL FOR THE STATE OF NEW SOUTH WALES
NICHOLAS BENDER SC, COUNSEL FOR EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF
AUSTRALIAN JEWRY; ZIONIST FEDERATION OF AUSTRALIA;
NATIONAL COUNCIL OF JEWISH WOMEN AUSTRALIA; NSW JEWISH
BOARD OF DEPUTIES; JEWISH COMMUNITY COUNCIL OF VICTORIA;
AUSTRALIA ISRAEL JEWISH AFFAIRS COUNCIL; THE DOR
FOUNDATION

<THE HEARING COMMENCED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Sherman.
MR SHERMAN: Commissioner, our first witness today is Dr Andre Oboler.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, good morning, Dr Oboler.
<ANDRE OBOLER, AFFIRMED
MR SHERMAN: Dr Oboler, have you given a second report to the Commission
dated 28 June 2026; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: I have, and it's absolutely huge.
MR SHERMAN: Well, thank you for the work that has obviously gone into that
report. Commissioner, the position with respect to the tender of this report requires
a little bit of explanation.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR SHERMAN: I would seek to tender the report at STAT.8999.0001.0405
together with a bundle of material referred to in that report, subject to the following.
There are some exhibits that are platform statements that are the subject of ongoing
confidentiality discussions. So it's proposed that those specific exhibits would not be
tendered at this stage but would, when those confidentiality issues are resolved.
I can indicate those exhibits to you. They are 3-059, 060, 064, 068, 083, 084 and
087. So, subject to not tendering those statements at this stage, we propose to tender
the balance of the materials.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. That is noted. Do I take it that the parties at the bar table
each have a copy of the exhibit list for today with the numbers?
MS SHARP SC: For the state of New South Wales, I don't have one yet, but
something has just been handed to me.
COMMISSIONER: If people are able to meaningfully follow the proceedings and
the tender, we need to make sure that each of the parties has a copy of that exhibit
list and then, Mr Sherman, I'm going to ask you to again indicate those items
identified as appendices that are not the subject of the tender at the present time.
Once that is done, people might be relieved to know I'm not going to give each an
individual exhibit number; the numbers will be as per the list.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly, Commissioner. I am told that a soft copy has been
provided but we are content to proceed in that way, and I can provide a general
indication that they are the platform statements.

COMMISSIONER: Right. Would you mind just running through?
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. So the exhibit numbers of 3-059, 060, 064, 068, 083,
084 and 087.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Is everyone content at the bar table that you now have an
understanding of what has just been tendered?
MR KAPLAN SC: Yes.
MS SHARP SC: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, good. Very well, Mr Sherman.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you, Commissioner. Dr Oboler, you have previously given
a statement to the Commission in Hearing Block 1; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: For the benefit of the transcript, I will just note that that statement
bears the document ID STAT.8999.0057.0022. That statement was dated 8 May
2026; is that right?
DR OBOLER: I believe that's right.
MR SHERMAN: And in that statement you gave evidence about the Online Hate
Prevention Institute and your role as founder and CEO of that institute; is that
correct?
DR OBOLER: That is correct.
MR SHERMAN: I don't need to go back to the detail of that statement but it's
correct that the Online Hate Prevention Institute is a charity and recognised leader in
tackling online antisemitism; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That is correct. Online hate in general and antisemitism in particular.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. You yourself hold a PhD in Computer Science from
Lancaster University in the United Kingdom; is that right?
DR OBOLER: That is correct.
MR SHERMAN: And a juris doctor and Bachelor of Computer Science with
Honours from Monash?
DR OBOLER: Correct.

MR SHERMAN: And you have served as the chair of the Global Policy Caucus of
the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: The IEEE, it's known as.
MR SHERMAN: Could you tell me a little bit about the pin that you are wearing on
your lapel today?
DR OBOLER: Yes. This pin is known as the Golden Core. It's the highest service
award from the IEEE Computer Society. That's the part that deals with computing
technology.
MR SHERMAN: And you are an expert member of the Australian Government's
delegation to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That is correct.
MR SHERMAN: And you've worked on efforts to combat online hate since 2004?
Is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That is correct.
MR SHERMAN: And you are also an Adjunct Associate Professor in the Law
School at La Trobe University; is that right?
DR OBOLER: Yes, that's correct.
MR SHERMAN: Dealing with your second report, which is the report we are here
to discuss today, by way of overview, the first aspect concerns the provision of
representative samples of antisemitic content across social media platforms; is that
right?
DR OBOLER: That's correct. I was asked to provide samples on seven specific
platforms, and the evidence covers that.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. And then the second question that was posed to you
asked you to provide observations on the overall responsiveness of platforms in
identifying and responding to the presence of antisemitic content in their services; is
that right.
DR OBOLER: Yes, that is correct.
MR SHERMAN: And the third question asked you to comment on material
differences in platform policies and reporting mechanisms; is that correct?

DR OBOLER: That's correct. I've answered that partly in the second question in
terms of individual platforms and how they respond and then summarised in that
third question the differences.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. In terms of the fourth to seventh questions, in general
terms, they asked you to provide comment on the policy and procedures adopted by
platforms, government responses, access to platform data and risks arising from
generative artificial intelligence; is that right?
DR OBOLER: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: Now, just before we get into the substance of your report and your
observations regarding the platforms, I wanted to ask you a few questions just to
understand the methodology that was used in obtaining and categorising the
antisemitic content that you've provided to the commission. Do you understand that?
DR OBOLER: I do, yes.
MR SHERMAN: Now, in your first report, you gave evidence that the Online Hate
Prevention Institute monitors the online environment to identify content that's
antisemitic. Could you just briefly recap what that monitoring involves?
DR OBOLER: Yes. So our monitoring approach is based on a time-based system.
So we apply the same amount of time monitoring each of the platforms using
a specific methodology. That methodology starts each hour of monitoring by doing
a search. We find an item of antisemitic content on the platform we are examining
for that hour. We capture that particular item, take a screenshot of it. If it's a video,
we download the video. We record the URL. The system automatically records the
current date and time, and it's classified according to our 27 different subcategories
of antisemitism.
Once that item has been recorded, we then go through the comments on that item,
checking them, capturing any of the comments that are antisemitic. When we are
done going through the comments, if the hour still has time left in it, then our staff
look for one of the people who engaged with it, either a comment or a like or a share.
They go and look at that person's profile, see in a very quick glance is there
something antisemitic that person's posted? If so, they capture it and start going
through the comments again and they keep snowballing in this way until the hour
finishes.
Once the hour is finished, they then move on to the next platform and they repeat the
process for an hour. We normally limit the staff to one to two hours a day doing this,
so one to two platforms. So this is how the sample is collected and then the sample
that has been provided to the Commission, there's two steps to it. We were asked for
a representative sample for each platform.

So what I did was I looked at the average number of items that we have for each of
our 27 subcategories on each platform. And then started with a sample size of 500
and said, proportionately, how many of each of these categories do we need, and
when it was coming out with a very small number, we rounded it up to six, just to
ensure there was enough data there to get a feel for it.
We did that for the first two platforms at the level of 500. Just due to time and cost,
we reduced it by half to 250 for the remaining five platforms. All of that data was
done by selecting it from the data we already had that came from June 2025 up until
the end of last month - end of the month before. And - sorry, no, yes, end of the
month before; we are now in July. And staff checked the items, found good examples
that represented each of the subtypes, filled in the slots, so we had to write the
number of examples for each subtype.
And then we have selected one item from each platform for each category to put into
the report itself as an example. So there's a lot more data that is in these appendices.
I suspect that is why I have two folders here; I think someone has printed them all
out.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. Just to clarify a few aspects of that methodology for
the sake of clarity, the examples that are maintained by OHPI are divided into 27
subcategories; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: 27 subcategories and those are subcategories of one of four sort of
major categories, and items can be in more than one subcategory and, therefore,
more than one major category.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. And the four main categories are Holocaust-related
material, incitement to violence, traditional antisemitism and Israel-related
antisemitism; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That's correct. I will clarify that the incitement to violence, it could
be violence. It does also include, for example, property damage, incitement to attack
synagogues, et cetera. So there's levels of harm there that may fall short of actual
violence to people but it's still in that sort of general category. And the last category,
traditionally we've called it Israel-related, but increasingly since 7 October 2023 it's
Israel/Israeli/Zionist/Zionism-related just as a general category.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. And you gave evidence on the last occasion that each
category except the Holocaust jokes category -
DR OBOLER: Yes.
MR SHERMAN: - that the parameters within which content is allocated to the
category are aligned or at least linked to the IHRA definition; is that correct?

DR OBOLER: Correct. The actual categories were made - sorry, the two IHRA
definitions. So the actual categories were made by the Australian experts to IHRA at
an IHRA meeting overseas, taking the two definitions, going through them and
effectively saying, okay, this line will be category 1. This example will be category
2. These few words will be category 3. So it's all directly linked back to the text in
either the IHRA Working Definition of Holocaust Denial and Distortion, which was
the first one, or the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, which was the
second one IHRA passed.
MR SHERMAN: In terms of that exercise that you just described regarding the
formulation of the specific categories into which content is allocated could you just
elaborate a little on the process that was followed to reach those parameters?
DR OBOLER: The IHRA experts - there were seven of us. I believe we were all
there. I believe it was the plenary in Rome. We sat around a table with the two
definitions and literally went through them line-by-line working out, you know, does
this line give us something new, in which case we add an extra category, or have we
already covered it, in which case we can move on to the next bit of the text. So it is
derived directly from the text. We started with the 26 categories directly derived, and
we added the Holocaust jokes when we found that they really didn't fit anywhere else
and needed their own category because some of the platforms were saying, well,
humour is an exception; it should be allowed, you know, even after Holocaust denial
was being banned. So we wanted to be able to count that separately and easily pull
that data out.
COMMISSIONER: In applying the IHRA definition in respect of anti-Israel
antisemitism, do you take regard of context?
DR OBOLER: Yes. The IHRA definition itself does require that context be taken
account of. There are categories - even in compiling data for the Commission, there
is things where we say, "This feels wrong, this looks highly problematic, but we
wouldn't call it antisemitism". We would say it's something else wrong with it but
not necessarily that.
There's also very peculiar cases not so much on the Israel ones but with some of the
Holocaust-related ones, a Nazi swastika and even our local neo-Nazi groups are not
always behaving in an antisemitic manner. So a swastika and a neo-Nazi who is, for
example, engaging in transphobia is not engaging in antisemitism at that point in
time. Even though the ideology is antisemitic, when you take into account the
context, they're actually doing something different in that instance.
MR SHERMAN: I'll come to the detail of the process by which these pieces of
content are recorded, but is one of the functions of selecting the 27 categories and
coding by reference to multiple categories that, in the ultimate data, the individual
instances can be aggregated and disaggregated down to the individual category
level?

DR OBOLER: Yes, correct, to the individual category and also we don't actually
code under the major categories. What we do is then analyse the data and say
anything that is coded under one or more subcategories that belong to a major
category count once under that higher level category.
MR SHERMAN: Yes. So as a consequence of that, the data to the extent that one
wished to exclude a particular subcategory can be recut in order to exclude that
subcategory from the broader dataset; is that right?
DR OBOLER: Yes. So one of the bits of analysis we do, and I don't recall off the
top of my - no, it was in the first report. There was a table. We looked at how many
of the items that were in category 4 and particularly in the category 4 item that refers
to denying Israel's right to exist by saying it's a racist endeavour, how many items
that fell within that category were not in another category as well. So how many of
them were only in our sample because they fell into that category.
And the answer was startling small. It was like a handful. And that can happen for
two reasons. One is because a particular statement might fall into two, so if you said,
you know, "Israel is a racist endeavour and we don't know about it because of Israel's
control of the media and it has no right to exist and therefore we should support
efforts to eliminate it", it's going to fall under both the control of media category and
it's going to fall under - I think it's 4.2, which is the "Israel has no right to exist
category" and it will also fall under 4.4, which is traditional antisemitism, in this case
the media category, but being applied to Israel.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. And in your first statement, you gave some evidence
about the cycles that you described earlier, being an eight-cycle exercise.
DR OBOLER: Yes.
MR SHERMAN: Could you speak a little about why the process is designed by
reference to hourly collection points?
DR OBOLER: Yes. Firstly, I will start off by saying the eight hours as I mentioned
last time is just because that's a standard work day of eight hours, was how we came
to that. Our initial collection after 7 October, we actually did 16 hours, but we did it
over a few months rather than all in one month. So that's the eight hours. The reason
for the one-hour periods, firstly, for any given platform, it spreads it out across the
month. It also divides it up. We have two analysts that actually do the collection, so
we have two different people exercising human judgment on half the sample each.
So that helps avoid any sort of biases or problems. But also with four cycles for each
of them, they're spreading it over the four weeks of the month, usually, and because
they're going through all the platforms before returning to the first one again, when
they start again, time has moved on.
They're starting with a new search. And it means if there was anything that was
biassing their initial search, they'd picked up an item that, for example, happened to

belong to a particular extremist group or something, the other seven samples are
unlikely to be in the same sort of echo chamber. So it means across the eight
samples, we should get a good representation.
MR SHERMAN: In terms of the searching exercise, can I just confirm a few details
with you. As I understand it, the coders apply an updated list of search terms to
identify content in the first instance; is that right?
DR OBOLER: That's correct, yes.
MR SHERMAN: When they find the content, they fill out a uniform data capture
form that records certain details; is that right?
DR OBOLER: That is correct.
MR SHERMAN: And they include the URL of the content, the URL of the user,
uploads of the screen capture or video and the category of online content against
which the content is being coded; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That's correct. There's a few other fields there that I mention in the
report. We do have field, for example, for comments. Again, going to your Honour's
comment about context, if there is something where the context is important and they
see the context, they can actually put it in comments so that we don't lose that
information. There's also a flag if the person looking at it thinks it's an inauthentic
account so, for example, a bot or something like that. They can flag that as well.
We do also actually have flags when they first capture it, there's a general flag to say
it's antisemitic, but something can be antisemitic and be against another group. So we
also have a flag for Islamophobia, for anti-LGBTQIA plus, for misogyny. So if it hits
multiple categories, we will capture that as well. And just in the case of
Islamophobia, we also have other subcategories. So, in that case, it would come up
first to code it with the antisemitism once and then to code it into a specific form of
Islamophobia.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. And in terms of the other types of information that is
collected, if there's a clear geographical nexus apparent from the piece of content, is
that recorded as well?
DR OBOLER: Correct. So we also do - we get them to look at the profile of the
person that posted it. If it's clear from the profile where the person is from, at the top
level, we have a couple of very broad geographic regions so, for example, North
America, Europe, et cetera. Australia, obviously, is its own one because that's
particularly significant for us.
So they flag it with that, but then there's another field where if there is a specific
location, they can put it in. And that could be a particular city, whether in Australia
or overseas. It can get very specific. That information either comes from the profile

itself that the person says, "This is where I am", or from the context of their content.
So it might be that their post is filled with AFL content, and we say, okay, this
person looks Australian. Or it's filled with Australian news commentary or things
and we say, yes, this looks Australian. It's not guaranteed to be perfect but it's
a pretty good guide.
MR SHERMAN: Your standard practice is at the point or the standard practice that
is followed is at the point that the content is recorded, it is also reported to the
relevant platform; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: Correct. The last step is to report it to the platform itself using their
internal processes, and I just add in the case of the data given to the Royal
Commission, we went back and re-reported everything last month. So it's all been
reported at least twice by us.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. You said the last step in the process is reporting.
DR OBOLER: Yes.
MR SHERMAN: After that point, the content is submitted to the system; is that
correct?
DR OBOLER: I would say it's usually - well, it could be. I would say it's probably
submitted to our system first before they report it, and then they move on to the next
item.
MR SHERMAN: At that point, there's a time and date stamp recorded on the
submission; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: Correct, yes.
MR SHERMAN: So it follows from that, does it, that the time and date stamp is
relatively contemporaneous to the report to the particular platform in your data?
DR OBOLER: Yes. Give and take a minute or so, yes.
MR SHERMAN: And the staff who undertake this data capturing and entry work,
they're trained for at least three months on technical aspects of the work and
definitions of antisemitism; is that right?
DR OBOLER: That's correct, yes.
MR SHERMAN: And testing is also conducted on the human coders by having
them categorise the same data as each other and then cross-referencing the results; is
that correct?

DR OBOLER: Yes. And we are currently training up new analysts to be able to do
that work as well.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. Now, turning to the exercise that you have performed
for the Commission, you have provided the Commission with a series of attachments
to your report that contain examples of antisemitic content that we referred to before;
that's correct?
DR OBOLER: Yes, and that's why, again, it's so huge. It's literally thousands of
examples that we have given. And I've got to say, for the Commissioner and others
that will be looking at this, it is quite intense, and, you know, we have had
a challenge for the team because we have looked at a lot more content in a shorter
period of time than we normally would. So it does have an impact.
MR SHERMAN: Before you referred to slightly different numbers of pieces of
content. It was 500 each for X and Meta, and 250 for the other platforms.
DR OBOLER: Correct. And that's the - that was the target. The actual number will
be a bit higher because, as I mentioned, some of those, on that sample size, it would
say we need one example or two examples. And we tried to increase those to
a minimum of six. There's a few categories where on some platforms there just
wasn't any data on that category. It's a very small sample. But, in general, I would
say we have at least 500, probably a few more and at least 250, probably a few more.
MR SHERMAN: You've also provided in addition to the attachments to your
statement an appendix with some examples to just give a flavour of the content as
part of your statement; is that correct?
DR OBOLER: That's correct. And those examples that are in the statement all come
from that sample. So there are IDs there to cross-reference them.
MR SHERMAN: To the broader dataset?
DR OBOLER: To the broader dataset. There are additional examples in my
statement that are not part of that dataset. So, for example, there was a collection of
data after the Bondi attack that we provided to Meta and that they then re-reviewed.
So we checked how many of those are still online and provided that data as well. So
there's another sample of - I forget how many hundred but it's in the report.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. Now, I might bring up an example to illustrate this
point. So if I can ask the operator to turn up STAT.8999.0001.0407_0030, which is
an example that has been taken from your appendix. Sorry, it should be 0030. So
focusing on the piece of content at the top of the screen here, do I take it from your
explanation before that this would have been screenshotted by one of the coders?
DR OBOLER: Correct.

MR SHERMAN: And then the material extracted from the spreadsheet at the
bottom is indicating that it was displayed on X, observed on 14 April 2026 at 9.20
am and 28 seconds and then removed by the 11 June; is that right?
DR OBOLER: Yes. I will just clarify that that "removed by", it may have been
removed as soon as 14 April. We knew it was there on 14 April. We can't tell when it
was removed between then and when we saw it was removed on 11 June. So it
doesn't mean it took that long, but somewhere in that period, when we rechecked it,
this content was no longer there.
MR SHERMAN: That's a function of X not making that type of information
available to the public, isn't it?
DR OBOLER: There may be an email that the analysts that first reported it would
have got, but we are reporting literally thousands of these things and trying to marry
those communications back up without a dashboard, which X doesn't provide, it
would be very hard. You know, if there was a reason to do it for one or two examples
we could probably put in the effort but we're talking hours’ worth of work to trace
one item.
MR SHERMAN: And some platforms don't -
DR OBOLER: Some platforms provide absolutely no information, even whether
they've actioned the report or not.
MR SHERMAN: Now, if I could turn to the next topic, which is - concerns your
evidence regarding platform responsiveness. As the head of an organisation that
systematically reports antisemitic material to platforms, have you made any
observations about the prevalence of content in general on the platforms?
DR OBOLER: Yes. So we - as I showed last time, we have graphs showing the
different levels of antisemitism on each platform overall, but then we can break that
down into the four major categories. So for each of the platforms we have looked at
in the report, what I've provided - I don't know if you want to pull one up - I have
provided a graph showing for each sample of data we collected, so for each eight
hours once a month since June and at various periods before that, what is the number
of items we were getting in each category at that point in time. And by plotting it
over time, we can actually see a graph of the levels rising and falling, and we can
different patterns on different platforms.
MR SHERMAN: Yes. And we might come back to some of the aggregate-level
reporting at a later stage, but if I could perhaps, to your invitation, take you to _0034
of your report. Sorry I should give the operator the proper ID
STAT.8999.001.0405_0034. Is this the platform-specific aggregate antisemitism -
DR OBOLER: This is the platform data for Facebook specifically. The first thing
we've got is the total number of items collected in those eight hours in each period

and, again, for some of them, we've scaled down to eight hours in order to make it
consistent. But, yes, you can see how, over time, the level that it rose
to - I mentioned before the sharp rise after 7 October. On Facebook, that just became
the new normal. And there's a number of points, you know, I point to particularly
January this year and April this year, which are actually significantly above even
what we saw after 7 October.
So that's, you know, that's a problem. If we look, then, at the bottom graph, that's
showing that same data but broken down into the four different types. So what we
can actually see there is a rise across multiple categories that lead to that result. So
you can see the spike in April, in fact, every single category went up that month and
that in aggregate leads to the total rise we see in the graph above.
MR SHERMAN: Could you give us a flavour of what is captured within the
traditional antisemitism category?
DR OBOLER: I don't know if you want to pull up the schema, but in general terms,
it covers a range of specific traditional antisemitic memes. So, for example, a global
Jewish conspiracy, Jews control the banks, Jews control government and government
institutions. Jews control the media. It also includes a generic traditional
antisemitism category which covers things like blood libel, things like deicide, I
think we've got one on there also - I think the dual loyalty may be in there or it may
be in category 4; I'd have to check. So, yes, there's a list that covers them. 3.6 is the
most generic one. That also captures things like racial slurs and those sorts of forms
as well.
COMMISSIONER: Dr Oboler, do you have an opinion about a causal link to the
high figure in April of this year?
DR OBOLER: I believe what we are seeing is the result of the Iran situation. So
there is a tie-in to events overseas. I believe other witnesses have mentioned that as
well. Although that's not always the case. Some of what we're seeing in our data,
particularly when we break it down, sometimes we see one form of antisemitism
increasing when others on the same platform are not increasing, which could indicate
that there's some sort of campaign or activism or something that is pushing it up from
a particular community of anti-Semites, if I can -
COMMISSIONER: On the graph we saw a moment ago, it looked to me as though
the graph for the anti-Israel antisemitism roughly followed the graph for the
traditional antisemitism. Does that suggest that frequently elements of both were
present or is it -
DR OBOLER: Not necessarily. There is some - there is some relationship because
some of the Israel-related antisemitism, particularly category 4.4, which is traditional
antisemitism applied to Israel or Zionists, it could be coded as both whatever form of
traditional antisemitism it is and also in category 4.4 as Israel related. So that will be
the same data item actually rising both of them at the same time. But it's also

possible - yes, so there's a certain per cent of that, but in this particular case, in April,
we were also seeing Holocaust-related content rise. We were also seeing violence
related content rise. So I would say while there is some overlap, it is more of, you
know, everything is rising.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you.
MR SHERMAN: Now, Dr Oboler, in your report, you've made some observations
for a number of platforms, both with respect to the trends in the content on the
platform and their responsiveness to reports. I was just going to take you through
each platform and give you an opportunity to elaborate on those observations. So if
we could start with X Corp, what are your observations about the prevalence of
antisemitic content on that platform and their responsiveness?
DR OBOLER: I might get you to actually give me the paragraph number, if I can
jump to it.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly.

of trust in the information upon which we make everyday decisions. So the
sociologist Niklas Luhmann has said in the absence of trust, it would be impossible
to get out of bed in the morning. But quite simply, you have to have expectations of
confidence in others to behave in certain ways that will, at the very least, not be
damaging to you and will potentially be good for you.
The trust literature tends to divide between what we might refer to as the
psychological and the sociological approaches. So trust can be a state of mind or
a belief or an expectation of particular individuals or groups. There are challenges in
aggregating that upwards. So is it meaningful to refer to trust in a whole society? We
can have different levels of trust in particular institutions, be they the media, the
courts, the corporate sector, and so on. So we use a proxy measure there for social
trust, which is that around social cohesion. And the Scanlon Foundation Index of
Social Cohesion established in 2007 and which was founded through Monash
University uses five metrics through which to measure social cohesion, including
belonging, worth, social inclusion and justice, participation, and acceptance or
rejection.
And as you noted, there has been a significant decline in the - those indices over the
last five years, which is also mapped by the work released earlier this year by the
Australian National University National Security College on its research into
Australian attitudes to national security risk and resilience, which found a significant
jump in concerns around national security. And, importantly, national security was
understood not simply in terms of traditional matrices of security, such as the
likelihood of foreign invasion for instance but also concerns around AI-enabled
threats, misinformation, threats to criminal infrastructure and economic threats, and
there was - there has been a very significant jump in concern about terrorism
between 2024 and 2026.
In terms of overall measures of trust, those such as the Edelman Trust Barometer,
undertaken by the Edelman Corporation for the last 25 years, has found that

Australia has middling levels of trust in its institutions, so ranked about 14th of the
28 countries surveyed, and that has been generally where Australia has sat. Although
I would say Australia has a significantly lower level of trust in its media than the
global average. Now, we may want to talk about how "media" is being defined there
because obviously the platform environment is increasingly constituting media as we
understand it. It's not simply traditional print media or broadcasting or news
publishers.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have developed a concept of what you described as
"mediated trust" to explain the process by which communications between
individuals within society are now mediated or directed through new methods of
communication, in particular, online communication. Could you elaborate on the
idea of mediated trust?
PROF FLEW: Certainly. The question of trust in distant others has been
a longstanding issue. So the reliance that - we have to have a reliance upon the
behaviours of others who we can't know. Okay? So if we need to get the bus or train
to work, that requires a certain level of trust in the bus driver or train driver to turn
up and deliver you to your destination. And you can't really know, nor should you
need to know anything about the bus driver or train driver's attitudes. You need to
have the confidence that they will acquit the task for which they're required to do so.
Now, in the information space, this means that increasingly we're reliant upon
institutional providers of information as the basis on which we make decisions. So
communications has moved from a primarily face-to-face activity, to unmediated at
different points of time through different technologies, and in the digital space in
which we now talk, those technologies have particular affordances that impact upon
how we understand trust, and so some of the concepts we will be talking about in this
inquiry, including algorithmic ranking of content, news generated content, the uses
of big data and so forth, increasingly inform the information which we receive.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thanks, Professor. Can I take you to the next part of your
report, which addresses opportunities for platform moderation and regulatory design,
and you've referred to a historical approach, as it were, where there's a three-part
approach to platform regulation based on legislation, regulation and what you've
described as governance. And you've made the observation in section 2.1 of your
report that it's been governance rather than government regulation that has been the
dominant mode of regulation for online technologies. And could you describe that,
please, that governance category, as it has been applied?
PROF FLEW: Certainly. So there has been a general trend towards governance, as
distinct from what's referred to in the literature as command and control regulation,
where multiple stakeholders, including non-government organisations, civil society
groups, academics and others are engaged in standard setting, and the idea is that it is
more around steering conduct as distinct from prohibiting certain types of activity
through government legislation.

Now, the internet has always linked itself to governance frameworks that, from the
point at which the internet becomes a popular many medium, if I was to put it that
way, which can be broadly dated from about 1994 to 1995, legislation is put in place,
most notably in the United States with the Communications Act, which establishes
that platforms are understood not to be media in the traditional sense, and this is
where the safe harbour provisions of the Communications Act, what's known as
section 230, become relevant here.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you are referring there to the United States
Communications Decency Act of 1996.
PROF FLEW: That's correct. And I would say that provided a template, at least in
the liberal democracy, so I would say about two-thirds of countries around the world,
for how the internet would be governed, broadly speaking.
MR LANCASTER SC: And there is no broadly applicable Australian equivalent
legislation to section 230 of the Communications Decency Act is there?
PROF FLEW: There is not. Section 5 and section 7, the Online Services
Amendments to the Broadcasting Services Act 1992, which were passed in 1998,
which set certain parameters around content online and around co-regulatory
frameworks, but I think it would be fair to say that their effectiveness has been
limited and, to some degree - I would say to some degree they've lapsed, I would say.
Although, one important point is they do give the Australian Communications and
Media Authority jurisdictional authority with regards to online content, which is
similar to countries such as the UK, where Ofcom was given similar powers, but
quite different to the United States where the Federal Communications Commission
by law does not have jurisdictional power with regards to online content.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. Just to perhaps descend into the detail of that for
a moment, the US provision that you referred to in section 230 says:
"No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the
publisher or speaker of any of the information provided."
That's the framework in which -
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: - the US has operated since 1996.
PROF FLEW: That's correct. And it was - at the time it was in relation to a case
with America Online. And it was at a time when the provider of the service was quite
distinct from the platform on which the content was created. So its equivalent would
be that if you're using Telstra broadband to access the internet at home, Telstra is not
legally liable for any content you post from that home. Now, as you would gather,

with content increasingly provided through platforms, that somewhat changes the
equation there, but it doesn't change the law itself.
MR LANCASTER SC: No, indeed. So in Australia there is, do you agree, no single
clear principle of that sort as applies in America but instead there are a number of
laws that apply to different parts of communications in Australia differently?
PROF FLEW: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: So, for example, in the context of defamation law, there is
a defence of innocent dissemination that a social media platform might take
advantage of if the defence conditions are met; yes?
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: But the Online Services Act does - which is also
a regulatory source of power for other aspects of what the social media platforms
provide, but there's nothing like the broad provision that applies in the United States.
PROF FLEW: There's not a broad category of exemption, but there are certainly
different legal frameworks based upon the platform upon which content is delivered.
So, for example, there are rules around election advertising that apply to television
and radio but which do not apply online.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have addressed in your report the challenges of
moderating harmful online content. Can I ask you about this. You have set it out in
section 3.1 of your report and you've identified seven particular challenges.
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could you just briefly address each of those please,
professor?
PROF FLEW: Certainly. I would just note that there is - overlaying this, there has
been a philosophical debate about whether the internet should be regulated. In the
Reno v ACLU case of 1996, Justice Dalzell observed with regards to the internet
that:
"...as the most participatory form of mass speech yet developed, the internet deserves
highest protection from governmental intrusion."
So there is always a debate around the legitimacy of government engagement in the
online space. At the same time, as we're aware from this Commission, online speech
can and does have real world consequences.
With regards to moderating harmful online content, as you asked, some of the issues
that arise are the scale and velocity. The volume of content uploaded to the internet

every second is phenomenon. It's estimated that six to eight hours of new video
content is uploaded to YouTube every second, just to take one example. The virality:
harmful content often goes viral within minutes, meaning that by the time a post is
flagged, reviewed and removed, that content has already been viewed by a very large
number of users and downloaded and shared and so on. Coded language is often used
to evade filters. Context is relevant here, and I believe the discussion with Dr Oboler
talked about some of the contextual issues.
The question of universal standards, and I will just note, I was also in 2011, 2012
chair of the Australian Law Reform Commission's review of the National
Classification Scheme, and this question of what is harmful arises in that context as
well, that there is content that is clearly illegal. There is also content which has the
potential to cause harm. And the second category is a difficult one around content
that is harmful but legal and the question of who is the arbiter of those questions
becomes important there.
So the question of universal standards, and standards vary over time. So I would say,
for instance, that while the National Classification Scheme has a lot of rules around
swearing, I would say there are now very few controls over swearing in media of any
form that I can think of. At the same time, new issues have arisen; say issues around
anorexia for example, is not something considered when the National Classification
Scheme was first developed.
There is also the point about the human costs of enforcement, that frontline
moderators face a very difficult task with high levels of psychological toll and high
burnout rates. And also the question of the risk - the risk of over-moderation, we may
want to return to that - but questions of legality, legitimacy, proportionality and due
process. So whereas, say, in the classification scheme - okay, let's say if a film is
banned the Australian Classification Board is required to document its reasons for
that, and those reasons can be appealed.
If a platform company takes down a particular piece of content, that may not be
known to those who posted the content, they may not be aware of the criteria, and
they may not have avenues to appeal that. Now, whether that is a good or a bad thing
may vary, but it's certainly quite different to how national classification schemes
have historically worked which has been around setting, I guess setting limits to
direct censorship.
MR LANCASTER SC: In that respect, I'm going back to the comment you made
about the absence or the challenge of determining the standards by which content are
regarded as - is regarded as harmful, though legal.
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You agree, I think, that digital platform companies are not
well placed to be arbiters of what is truthful.

PROF FLEW: They would certainly say that themselves. Mark Zuckerberg, in his
first appearance before the US Congress, questioned whether Facebook should be, as
he put it, an arbiter of truth.
MR LANCASTER SC: Were there any other aspects to your view that they are not
well placed to be arbiters of content?
PROF FLEW: I think that decisions are made all the time, and when I say
"decisions" there may also be non-decisions. But I think that the bases on which
those decisions are made - I would not say - I would not say that they're arbitrary but
I would also say that the bases on which the decisions are made are open to debate.
There's not clearly grounded constitutional bases for them or directives from
government. There's a view of what is - what is reasonable.
MR LANCASTER SC: You've described one of the frameworks for moderating
online harmful content as involving soft law.
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you've referred to your view that, broadly speaking,
this is the approach adopted by the eSafety Commissioner under the Online Safety
Act. Could you explain that, please?
PROF FLEW: I should say being in a room full of lawyers and being a non-lawyer
myself, I feel slightly intimidated in answering a question about what any particular
form of law is. But as Ari Friedberg has observed, soft law occupies a middle
position between no government interference at one end and complete government
involvement at the other. It typically involves the application of codes, standards,
protocols, boards of review - means by which there are - they're typically forms of
self-regulation but I don't think that the term "self-regulation" captures all forms of
soft law.
So the concept has its origins in areas like international shipping where there is not
a single global entity that can govern the seas but there are a set of treaties, protocols,
understandings, et cetera, through which questions like, for instance, which
countries' boats have the right to ship - to fish in certain waters are determined and
these three examples are what's known as soft law.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you include as what you described as the safety by
design principles as part of that?
PROF FLEW: Safety by design is, at the moment, something of an open concept. It
was articulated in the Statutory Review of the Online Safety Act 2021 undertaken by
Delia Rickard. And it's also, for some time, informed the practice of the Office of the
eSafety Commissioner; the Office of the eSafety Commissioner being established in
2017 by the - the intention, as put by the minister at the time, of having a more agile

regulatory framework than that provided through the legislative instruments that the
Australian Communication and Media Authority drew upon.
So I mentioned earlier the extension of the Broadcasting Services Act to online
services, the sense that that was not really fit for purpose, and that a different entity
was required that could be empowered to work more collaboratively with relevant
companies. And safety by design is, in part, around the principle of, I guess, you
might say ratcheting up standards by working with the companies around design
decisions made on their platforms that can improve the user experience while also
addressing online harms, and possibly being good for the commercial interests of the
companies themselves.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have also referred to relatively recent developments in
the UK and in the EU and you address the EU's Digital Services Act and the UK's
Online Safety Act, and your report goes on to address the Rickard Review and
Australia's recommendations in respect of a digital duty of care. Could I ask you just
to address one particular aspect of the UK Online Safety Act as a comparator for
what might be Australia's future? You have noted that the UK Online Safety Act in
its form as legislated involves a series of multiple narrower duties rather than one
general digital duty of care. Could you explain your view about the relative merits of
that approach?
PROF FLEW: Yes. Those who originally proposed the idea of a duty of care
approach to regulation, Woods and Perrin, envisaged the idea that it would be
an overarching framework that sets out a set of principles around which companies
engaged in the online space should operate, but in which the capacity to set both the
means by which those were achieved and what might be the principles had a degree
of flexibility over time.
Now, in the seven-year history of the Online Safety Act going from being initially
proposed to being finally implemented, it adopted a series of narrower duties. So
there was a sense that there was a degree of legislative creep, if you like, that it was
felt legislation has to address this and this and this. And one consequence of that has
been that the risk framework requires that risk is defined in terms of the law itself,
whereas the original intention behind the duty of care was that there would be
a greater degree of flexibility on the part of the regulator to determine where a risk
might arise.
MR LANCASTER SC: And as a matter of principle, do you have an opinion about
the preferable approach to be adopted?
PROF FLEW: I think the lesson of this space is that there's always going to be,
ultimately, a hybrid approach to regulation; that there are pros and cons to each
framework. The challenge with - and there are a series of challenges with
a legislative framework, partly that legislation is difficult to amend once enacted. So
when situations change, the process through which legislation is amended is, you
know, is complex and time consuming and may not - may not happen.

The soft law approach has the virtue of being more agile. Companies involved would
argue that they are best placed to understand what the issues are and, therefore, need
to be engaged in the process of addressing the issues. The concern is that the
combination of soft law and self-regulation can produce something that might be
very soft indeed, particularly if the entities tasked with overseeing the laws lack
sufficient distance from the entities which they're regulating.
So, ultimately, there tend to be hybrid approaches. Also, I should say, informed by
human rights considerations which, you know, need to be foregrounded in any
attempt to propose legislative solutions.
MR LANCASTER SC: In part of your report dealing with the development of
telecommunications legislation, you've referred to the Digital Industry Group in 2019
being asked by the Federal Government to develop a Voluntary Disinformation Code
of Practice with the idea that it might operate as an adopted code in similar form to
a structure that advised in the European Union and you refer to the Communications
Legislation Amendment (Combatting Misinformation and Disinformation) Bill that
the Federal Government initially proposed but then withdrew in November 2024.
You've said that the absence of federal legislation in this area is a notable gap. Could
you explain what the effect of that gap is on the publication of misinformation and
disinformation online?
PROF FLEW: Yes. The movement towards a Voluntary Disinformation Code of
Practice was in line with the soft law approach, that it was hoped that, I guess,
enlightened self-interest might prevail in this space without the heavy hand of
government needing to come in. The difficulty in implementing the code was that
where a breach was found against one of the initial signatories, they simply didn't
feel themselves to be governed by the code. And there was no real capacity then to
act to apply sanctions to the company involved, which was X formerly known as
Twitter.
In light of that, there was a proposal that government should have reserved powers to
register industry codes, enforce industry code compliance and make standards
relating to the activities of digital platforms. So Misinformation and Disinformation
Amendment was proposed. This found itself friendless in the Senate, I think might
be a way to summarise it, that it was opposed both by the Liberal-National Party
Coalition, who saw it as unduly impinging upon freedom of speech. It was also
opposed by the Australian Greens who felt it didn't do enough to address the power
of tech companies. And it was criticised by the Australian Human rights
Commissioner in being overly broad in its definition of misinformation and
disinformation, setting an unacceptably low threshold for what constituted harm and
placing excessive powers over online content with the ACMA.
Now, the virtue of a piece of legislation in this space, to my mind, is the capacity to
define what misinformation and disinformation might be, because the challenge that
continually arises around categories like online harm, misinformation, et cetera, is

the question of what is in the eye of the beholder. So to my mind, the capacity - the
existence of a legislatively defined instrument that can state what can or can't
constitute misinformation or disinformation would be an advance in terms of
regulating online harm, but given the critical realities, I think it's unlikely that
a misinformation bill will return to the parliament at any time in the near future. So
we would be looking at other, other options in that regard, in which a digital duty of
care may well be relevant too.
MR LANCASTER SC: As a preferable mechanism by which to approach the
problem?
PROF FLEW: As a different - whether it's preferable, we'll see, but as
a different - different mechanism to approach the problem.
COMMISSIONER: In some respects, Professor, a code in respect of
misinformation might impose a greater burden on the freedom of political
communication than a code dealing with hate speech, depending on the definition of
the latter. Would you agree with that?
PROF FLEW: It could, yes. Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You provided an analysis of a particular example of the
spread of misinformation or disinformation online in the context of the Russia
invasion of Ukraine. I'm not going to ask you to go through all the detail of the table
that you have provided but could you identify what you draw as the lesson from that
international example?
PROF FLEW: Okay. What I would draw as the lesson is that self-regulation is
ultimately limited, that it may lack transparency. There's the question of
independence; there's the question of enforcement criteria and the voluntary nature of
involvement. So I think there's the need for a step beyond self-regulation.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are referring there to self-regulation by social media
platforms of -
PROF FLEW: Yes, self-regulation by companies themselves. Self-regulation
through principles-based regulation, there's the interesting experiment, I guess, of the
Meta Oversight Board, formerly the Facebook Oversight Board, which was
established in 2021 and which there are Australian representatives on the board
which has undertaken a form of what I call third-party quasi-self-regulation in that it
has a series of esteemed panellists from throughout the world on it, who adjudicate
on content moderation decisions with the idea that this creates a body of case law
that can subsequently be appealed to, and which aims to address the problem of
a platform not wanting to itself be the arbiter of truth but which can draw upon
expertise. And it is funded in trust in a manner that separates the funding of the board
from the operations of Meta itself.

In practice, it moves quite slowly, I think it would have to be fair to say, about the
Oversight Board. There's also the question of the different environment in which the
company now perceives itself to be operating in in 2026, as distinct from 2019, 2020
when the board was first established. But it's a very interesting innovation in a kind
of self-regulation that can potentially have some kind of legal authority and some
kind of teeth. But certainly nation state regulation can have teeth. The question is
ensuring that it's compliant with human rights law and obligations.
I will just mention there that some talk about - I mentioned the European Union
earlier. There was a speech the French President François Mitterrand gave to the
Internet Governance Forum in 2018 where he identified the possibility for the
European Union being something of a third way, as he put it, between Silicon
Valley, self-regulation and high state regulation of the kind we find in the People's
Republic of China. And the EU is often referred to here where we're looking for
mechanisms that have some kind of a balance between, if you like, completely free
market approaches and highly state-controlled approaches.
MR LANCASTER SC: And your indirect reference a little earlier to the change of
regulatory atmosphere in the United States in 2026, could you elaborate on that?
PROF FLEW: The second Trump presidency and the very strong alliance between
many of the leading tech companies and that presidency.
MR LANCASTER SC: To your observation, has that involved a renewed emphasis
on the absolute nature of the entitlement of social media platforms to publish
content?
PROF FLEW: I - it certainly involved the dismantling of a range of mechanisms
that had been applied within the companies, such as the operation of Trust and Safety
Councils.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. In the next section of your report on hostile
misinformation online, you have referred to the hostile misinformation effect. Could
you explain what that is and how it's relevant to an understanding of what occurs
online, which is itself necessary to understand how to regulate it.
PROF FLEW: Sure, most certainly. It builds upon what is a long-established
concept of the hostile media effect which is that two individuals with different
political or other orientations can view the same piece of information and perceive it
to be balanced or biased quite differently. And so the perceptions of - so perceptions
of bias, this is the question around can you get an objective measure of bias that
differentiates itself from perceptions. And the authors involved in this European
study argue that this has translated to the online space where people will perceive the
information environment as being particularly hostile to their own perspective or
point of view.

It's also quite likely to be co-exist with which party is in government. So
a symposium that took place at Griffith University in Brisbane last week produced
a report on trust in government - yes, trust generally but also trust in government,
which found that in the current survey, Labor voters were twice as likely to trust
government as Coalition voters. Now, I dare say if you had a different government,
that figure may flip the other way around. I don't think it's something that's intrinsic
to the people surveyed as distinct from their likelihood of perceiving government to
be more trustworthy if the government that they elected is in power.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have also addressed, perhaps, the other side of the coin
or at least another relevant aspect is the psychological motivations behind those who
provide or publish misinformation.
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could you address what you have said in your report about
that?
PROF FLEW: Well, I picked up on Dr Oboler's comments earlier that, in some
instances, it is motivated by a kind of in-group identity and social media can amplify
the construction in-group identities by promotion of posts that are perceived to be
hostile to the perceived outgroup, that social media platforms can particularly
promote that form of affective polarisation. It also can be quite simply around
money.
So in the studies of fake news, there was the famous Macedonian teenagers who
suddenly were driving Mercedes around the village on the basis they had identified a
way to game YouTube for Trump supporters with content that would bring
advertising to them, that, hence, they had a Mercedes. Whether they were
particularly invested one way or another in the content they were posting was quite
a different question. It was primarily a commercial interest.
MR LANCASTER SC: When you are addressing psychological motivations, you
also refer to the fact that there's yet another category of poster who may simply have
a willingness to be disruptive or non-conscientious rather than actually holding
a view consistent with the information that's being published.
PROF FLEW: Yes. There is the question of whether people say things online that
they wouldn't actually say to the same person or group were they in a face-to-face
environment.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that itself might have different psychological drivers?
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have recommended in your report that to the extent
that nation-state governments have a role in setting content moderation rules and

guidelines, you consider there are five principles that should govern their activity or
their actions. Could you address each of those briefly, please?
PROF FLEW: Certainly. So the five principles are legality, legitimacy,
proportionality, due process, and harmonisation to the greatest degree possible. So
the principle of legality is that terms of service should be clear and comprehensive;
and that any applications of restrictions on online speech should be based on
clear - clear, legally clear criteria.
Legitimacy - and this is where - the question of whether platforms can effectively
self-regulate partly comes around the legitimacy question. You know, are there
avenues to appeal? Is there due process in decision-making? And so forth. And also
that remedies should be proportionate to the matters, the matters raised, and to
guarantee online and offline security without unduly inhibiting upon freedom of
speech and that some form of due process exists. And that to the greatest agree
possible, nation states should look to harmonise their laws and regulations in this
space with other certainly comparable nation states and international law.
MR LANCASTER SC: And by that are you referring to the European and UK
examples or just as a general principle?
PROF FLEW: Yes, as a general principle. So, you know, whether it be the various
United Nations Conventions; some of the principles that have been developed by
international non-government organisations, such as the Manila principles, the Santa
Clara principles. And, yes, certainly given that the platforms involved operate across
multiple jurisdictions, the extent to which we can minimise pressures towards what's
referred to as the splinternet - where if you go to a different place you are dealing
with a different internet to the one you dealt with back home - so for instance not
being able to access the New York Times in Beijing or whatever it might be - that we
aim to minimise the extent to which - given that, you know, one of the greater virtues
of the internet is this capacity to operate as a global network, that we aim to
harmonise laws and regulations.
COMMISSIONER: Generally, do VPNs create a difficulty in that regard? So that if
Australia imposes particular regulation, would you expect that that could be readily
avoided by someone in Australia using a VPN?
PROF FLEW: It can. It certainly can. I mean, this one comes up most notably
around pornography. It certainly - it certainly can. I guess the point would be that the
existence of the law provides some capacity to deem that to be in breach, in breach
of the law.
MR LANCASTER SC: Professor, you've provided a series of recommendations in
your conclusion. We have addressed, I think, most of them in the course of the
questions I've asked, and they can perhaps speak for themselves. But you've referred
to the co-regulatory approach in which self-regulation alone will not achieve an
appropriate outcome?

PROF FLEW: Yes. There may be an opportunity here with the pending digital duty
of care response of the Federal Government to the Rickard Review, in that it
provides - it provides the capacity to reinstate, if you like, principles of social licence
and align those to questions of best practice. I think there is potentially an
opportunity here.
That the challenge - the challenge with the self-regulatory models is always: Well,
what happens if some entity chooses to simply ignore them? Where does legal teeth
exist? And there may be capacity through a revised Digital Duty of Care Act to put
some kind of legal teeth there, while at the same time promoting principles around
social licence for platforms that are keen to work with governments and others,
around the matters of public concern they're addressing.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you to address specifically your sixth conclusion
and recommendation where you say:
"It's important for governments to actively support tufted sources of information."
PROF FLEW: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can you just elaborate on that?
PROF FLEW: Sure. Well, I think there's - we don't want the existing news media
infrastructure to collapse. We - and when I say "we", let's say do. But I've concluded
a study on the sustainability of news, news publishers, and a book that's recently
come out called Valuing News which addresses this; that the News Media
Bargaining Code has been one instrument through which this has happened, that it's
effectively - it's a requirement that the major digital platforms, being Meta and
Google in the first instance, reach agreements with news publishers around payment
for redistribution of content. That's been extended to a news media bargaining
initiative.
There's some debate about whether all platform companies are going to comply with
that. I think, over time, we're possibly looking at government support for commercial
news. I think that in addition to funding for the ABC and SBS I think that questions
around news deserts, around the loss of jobs in journalism and the loss of news
infrastructure are going to be become - not going to, are pressing at the moment. And
the question of what - it's not apparent that the market itself can solve the problem.
So we know enough now about the bases of subscriptions to know that subscriptions
will provide a basis for some media but not all media.
