antisemitism. Is it standard practice for ISD to adopt that definition in its policy
work?
MS ROSE: We use the IHRA definition as a useful framework for understanding
online antisemitism. When we analyse antisemitism on a large basis, using big data
approaches on social media, we find it to be the most useful instructive working
definition for understanding content which, in context, may be antisemitic. And we
refer to those 11 examples there. We've looked at a range of definitions. They are
sometimes useful and sometimes less useful. Ultimately, when you are and our
analysts are coding hundreds of lines or thousands of lines of antisemitic posts, no
one definition speaks to the entire environment. So we use the IHRA definition as
a useful working tool in combination with our own definition of hate.
MR BESHARA: For the purposes of this report, you deemed it appropriate to use
that definition in a flexible way with regard to context; is that fair?
MS ROSE: Yes, exactly.
MR BESHARA: I might begin, then, with the first broad topic that your report
examines, namely, the scale and the nature of antisemitic hate online. You note in the
report that antisemitism is amplified by a range of diverse ideological movements,
and you identify three in particular, namely, far right individuals, groups and
networks forming one category; far left antisemitic groups, and Islamist extremist
actors. Can you give an overview of those various sources of antisemitic conduct and
actors?
MS ROSE: Yes, absolutely. So we have considered those three ideological
communities as places that antisemitism can be found. Building on that, we also look
at the across the mainstream and also the role of hostile states in promoting and
boosting antisemitic content. Speaking specifically to the far right, antisemitism is
a very integral part of far-right ideology in many cases. We see a large network of
online groups, individuals and diffuse networks who regularly promote white
supremacist or far-right versions of antisemitic ideology. Often, that leads to and
promotes specifically violence against Jewish communities.

On the far left, we have considered here that, in our report, that far-left antisemitism
can often take a more covert manner where it's less overtly antisemitic, but
individuals contribute to a wider environment which erodes Jewish publication in
public life and often where it strays into the conflict and the debate around criticism
of Israel in the context of the war - which is, of course, by no means inherently
antisemitic but can be expressed in antisemitic ways. And that is one of the more
common forms of antisemitism that we see on the far left. And then, of course,
antisemitism is equally integral to Islamist online environments, where commonly
Jewish people are demonised, viewed as inferior based on a supremacist world view
and targeted on that basis.
MR BESHARA: In your report, you refer to a phenomenon of cross-ideological
hybridisation whereby these groups which, in some respects, are ideologically
opposed to one another, find common cause in expressions of antisemitism. Can you
elaborate on that phenomenon?
MS ROSE: Yes. I think the kind of neat bucket which I just discussed, the
ideological communities, is a useful analytical approach, but in practice, it's quite
a lot messier than that in the online environment. Previously, we would consider,
before the social media age, formal groups, top-down networks in which extremist
communities would operate. Nowadays, it's a lot more diffuse. Individuals can
access lots of different forms of antisemitism, lots of different ideological
communities quite readily. What that leads to is this form of ideological mixing,
which we refer to hybridisation, where an individual can almost pick and mix
different forms of antisemitism from different networks.
That has included previously - and we saw this particularly immediately after the
October 7 attack - different ideological actors who don't necessarily have that much
in common, such as far right and Islamist networks, uniting around a shared
antisemitic core. They would say, "We know we don't have much in common but we
are going to put those differences aside for the moment because the core enemy is
the Jewish community".
MR BESHARA: What role does the online environment play in facilitating that
cross-ideological hybridisation?
MS ROSE: The key point to make is access. Whereas an individual previously
wouldn't necessarily have ready access to extreme forms of hate, unless you would
know of a specific group in a top-down way, nowadays, very harmful content is
highly accessible to any individual who picks up a phone. That can be through
mainstream social media platforms where this content is available, also through
fringe communities where there are fewer safeguards and it's very easy to access
very, very harmful content.
MR BESHARA: What is the causal role, if any, of encrypted messaging platforms
in fuelling that?

MS ROSE: The online antisemitism environment, we refer to it as a "tech stack". So
that's a layering of multiple different forms of mainstream platforms, fringe
platforms, end to end encrypted messaging services, gaming services, which
extremists use for different purposes. In the same way that each of us might use
Facebook for a different way we'd use X to a different way we'd use LinkedIn, it's
the same with extremists. And so they might use a mainstream platform for serving
a more palatable form of their ideology, then funnelling the user into increasingly
harmful, less moderated spaces, more high harm spaces and, in some cases, these are
end to end encrypted messaging networks where the platform itself has very little
idea of what is going on on that platform. These are closed spaces which we have
seen to be particularly harmful, particularly for children who are able to be funnelled
into these spaces and there are very, very few safeguards in those online spaces.
MR BESHARA: And you referred to more palatable forms of antisemitic content
online. I take it by that you are referring to the use of memes, coded language and
other ways of expressing antisemitic sentiment that might evade strict content
moderation policies?
MS ROSE: Exactly. So we see the extremists and antisemitic actors use different
codes. For example, they will change a letter in a word to a number to avoid content
moderation. They'll use emojis. They'll use memes. So a lot of inferred humour there
and inferred antisemitism which is only necessarily identifiable to an individual who
knows the context of that meme already and is able to interpret it in that way. And
that is one way in which not only is antisemitism normalised and violence is
normalised, but they're able to evade moderation practices.
And antisemitism is not always illegal. It's not always in violation of platforms' terms
of service. Extremist actors are quite good at knowing what it does and doesn't cross
the line, and so they're able to just stay under that line of detection on a mainstream
platform, but then on another platform or, for example, on a podcast might express
a more overt or clearly harmful version of that sentiment.
MR BESHARA: In your report at paragraph 13, you express the view that platforms
struggle to effectively respond to even the most overtly violent and antisemitic
content, and you cite the specific example of analysis by the ISD in the period after 7
October 2023, which involved examining about 130 posts on X glorifying terrorist
violence, and then following up days later after the content had been reported and
finding that the vast majority of it was still online. Now, can you give your opinion
as to why it is that even clearly violative content of that kind remains online,
notwithstanding that it's been reported to the platforms as in violation of their terms
of service?
MS ROSE: I can't necessarily tell you why. I think you would have to ask the
platform. What we have seen over a sustained period - and this is just one example of
the type of experiences of the failures of moderation, which not only ISD has seen
but a number of civil society organisations and communities have seen - is that either

the terms of service, so the community guidelines, aren't relevant to the online
landscape which is continually evolving. Or they're not effectively enforced. That
could be due to the automated moderation system again not being continually
updated on the types of antisemitic or violative content available. Or it could be
because the human moderators aren't trained to identify that form of illegal content
or hate speech or terrorist content. In this case, I couldn't guess as to why the
platform wasn't able to identify branded Hamas content and remove it in a timely
manner.
MR BESHARA: And we will get to the various techniques of content moderation in
a moment, but staying with the work that ISD did around 7 October, can you give us
a sense of how antisemitic content online has changed in terms of its volume, its
content and its nature since 7 October?
MS ROSE: So immediately after the 7 October attack, we set out to analyse the
volume of antisemitic content on YouTube videos about the conflict, and we found
a 51-fold increase in the volume of antisemitic content on those videos. Of course,
suffice to say that the number of videos went up, so it's reasonable that the number of
comments went up, although there would, of course, have been videos about the
conflict before 7 October. But even proportionately to the number of videos, we
found an increase - I think we found a 2.5 per cent increase proportionately to the
number of videos.
So the kind of antisemitism, counter-antisemitism sector largely will think about 7
October as letting antisemitism out of the box. Since 7 October, we have seen a rise
across mainstream and extremist platforms, a rise in attacks against Jewish
communities globally. We have seen communities isolated from civil society and it's
had that chilling effect on communities and therefore eroded their ability to
participate in civic life and in democracy writ large.
So we have this whole what we call a long tail of harms. We are keen to not just
think about this issue as the promotion and mobilisation of violence from online
spaces, but consider the wider impacts of extremism - not just violent extremism but
wider extremism on the Jewish community, and we have been able to evidence that
with our work through communities around the wide range of harms to them.
MR BESHARA: Addressing that long tail of harms that you mentioned, you talk in
your report about the importance of upstream prevention strategies in particular. Can
you elaborate on that?
MS ROSE: Exactly. So we refer to the public health model for violence prevention
or for countering hate. And here you can - if you think about antisemitism, for
example, as a virus, you would have three tiers of how you respond to a public health
incident such as the pandemic. So in the primary tier, you would look to build
resilience among society to that disease. In the secondary tier, you would look to
treat those who have become slightly ill, with, for example, a drug or a rehabilitative

measure. And then in the tertiary tier, you would look to rehabilitate those who have
been ill back into a healthy community.
We can think about it in the same way for violence prevention or antisemitism
prevention, and this is an increasingly common approach in the sector and among
governments as well, which makes sure we look at this range of engagement with
antisemitism, not just violence prevention itself. So in a primary tier, you would want
to consider things like digital literacy training, inoculation or pre-bunking of
antisemitic beliefs. That's not just for children; it's also for adults and considering the
ways in which adults can engage with social media in a more pro-social way.
In the secondary tier, we look primarily at counter-narrative or counter-speech
campaigns and how we can deliver those more effectively. And then the tertiary tier,
it's often off-ramping, one on one support to those who have been very involved in
highly harmful movements. So this approach, this public health approach, looks to
address all those things at one. What we often see on a policy level is that these
policy areas can be quite siloed. So you will have your counter-terrorism, law
enforcement, intelligence services not necessarily understanding their role or
working with people working on cohesion interfaith also siloed from digital and the
regulatory approach.
And so what we are always trying to encourage is increasing cross-government
collaboration to understand all the sectors that are involved in the prevention of
antisemitism and how they can increasingly cooperate in this more diffuse online
environment where threats are coming from more places than they previously did.
MR BESHARA: And this links with another concept in your report about the
post-organisational nature of the antisemitism landscape. Could you elaborate on that
briefly?
MS ROSE: Exactly. So 10 or 20 years ago when you think about extremist
movements, you would think about groups with a leader, regular offline meetings.
Often, that would be quite ideologically top down. So if you think about Islamist
groups, for example, they might still operate in this way where there's an ideology
which is filtered through the organisation. Now, though, the online environment
doesn't function as a set of groups. It functions as a diffuse network of individuals,
chats, online groups spaces, which is a lot messier than it previously was, meaning
that individuals can engage in a bit of antisemitic ideology or a bit of an extremist
movement without necessarily being a fully-fledged member. Membership doesn't
look like what it used to. There's no such thing as being a member of an online
network in the same way.
However, what we often find is that the policies that were built to respond to
extremism, often in the post 9/11 environment, take a group-based approach. If you
can think about terrorist prescription group models, they look to identify a group and
ban it. Now, that's not an unhelpful approach, but it won't meet the challenge of the

online environment where lots of these individuals and the majority of this content
doesn't come from formal groups; it comes from individuals, networks, online chats.

MS ROSE: Yes. So we sought out to try and understand the trends in antisemitism

I'm cautious to note here that that is likely an underestimate of the overall volume of
antisemitic content in Australia, because the majority of users, you would imagine,
do not identify themselves on the platform structures as located in Australia.
Typically, for example, on 4chan or on Telegram, a lot of users would be anonymous
and wouldn't need to enter that information.
We include here only five platforms: 4chan, specifically 4chan's "/pol/" board, which
is short for politically incorrect. It's a known space where extremist networks
operate. X, Tumblr, extremist forums and extremist blogs, we use these platforms,
and it's clear that this is an omission of a number of mainstream and large platforms
where antisemitism operates, because these are the only platforms where we were
allowed to collect data based on location or where an individual could note their
location. I can dive later on a bit deeper into those data access issues that we faced.
We -
MR BESHARA: And just in terms of - sorry, I didn't mean to cut you off.
MS ROSE: We identified nearly 42,000 posts over that year period. We did this
using a classifier which we trained using subject matter expertise and ethnographic

posts that we surfaced. It's not - and we couldn't say whether it's accurate to the
number of posts overall because we don't have, again, access to that data but I
would happy to talk through some of the indications they gave us about the volume
of antisemitism over time.
MR BESHARA: Yes, let's do that. So in your analysis of the data, you note that
there are two large spikes in antisemitic content on 13 and 22 June 2025. Can you
just speak to that briefly?

MS ROSE: Yes. So the 13 June 2025 was the day that Israel attacked Iranian

Iran. And on 22 June was when the US joined in. So it's clear that those spikes in
antisemitic content from Australian users - and when we did a manual qualitative
analysis of the posts from those individual days, we found that there was a high level
of discussion around the Middle Eastern conflict. This is not necessarily a surprising
finding. We found this across a number of research reports, and other organisations
have found similar findings, that antisemitic incidents globally but also volume of
antisemitism on social media peaks around key moments in the Middle East conflict,
and we found that particularly around the Iran war.
MR BESHARA: I think you mentioned there was another spike associated with the
assassination of Charlie Kirk on 10 September?
MS ROSE: Yes, exactly. We saw an elevated volume of antisemitism on that day,
discussions of the alleged - or the conspiratorial alleged role of Israel in that
assassination and making antisemitic claims based on conspiracy theories that Israel
had assassinated Charlie Kirk. This, to me, speaks to the relevance of international
events to the Australian conflict. Of course, any user based in Australia can access
any content globally and so this isn't necessarily based on national borders, but, to
me, this speaks to the importance of being able to operate globally in response to
antisemitism and international cooperation with other states who are facing similar
issues.
MR BESHARA: I might just take you to the next page of the report which contains
another useful chart. So this is the data disaggregated by platform and you can see

MS ROSE: This speaks to the tech stack that I was describing before where an
individual doesn't use only one platform for only one purpose but engages in a wide
range of platforms, and any individual platform approach to this issue will likely fail
where there is an ecosystem of social media platforms, providers, gaming services,
which function together to exacerbate the issue of antisemitism from extremist
networks in particular, but also from mainstream communities.
4chan's /pol/ board here is well documented as hosting extremist networks,
particularly on the far right. What I should say here that these - again, this is only the
data that we have been able to surface in this analysis. This doesn't necessarily speak
to the overall volumes on these platforms, and we would want to also, if we had
access to that data, be able to include other platforms where we know antisemitism
exists. But this is a clear indicator here that regulatory approaches and
counter-measures against antisemitism can't only focus on mainstream platforms;

they have to take into account the role of fringe platforms in the very high harm
forms of antisemitism that they produce as well.
MR BESHARA: And before I take you to some of those possible regulatory
responses, including greater access to data for researchers, I might just have you
comment on the role of recommender systems and algorithmic amplification which
you address in your report, and how they drive antisemitism online?
MS ROSE: So platform recommender algorithms serve content to users who would
not otherwise have seen it. That is part and parcel of social media platforms' business
model, to increase engagement and keep you on the platform longer,
effectively - with all forms of content, not just with harmful content. We recent
conducted a study with the Antisemitism Policy Trust, which is a charity here in the
UK, to understand the role of recommender algorithms in serving antisemitic content
specifically to minors. So we created 10 users of 15 year old people, 15 year old kids
here in the UK, five boys, five girls and prompted each of those users with a different
set of indicators.
For example, two were prompted on generic right-wing ideas and beliefs. Two of
them were prompted on generic left-wing ideas and beliefs. One was prompted on
some extremist codes just to see what would happen. One was prompted based on
manosphere or male lifestyle influencer key words. So none of these key words have
anything to do with the Israel Palestine conflict, with Jewish people or with
antisemitism. We trained the account initially to make sure that the platform
understood that it was a 15 year old, so we were getting generic pranks in school,
teachers, that kind of content.
We then entered the search terms that we had identified, watched the top three videos
relevant to those search terms and then went back to the For You page and just
scrolled and watched fully any videos that were relevant to the conflict, potentially
relevant to antisemitism as we will. We repeated that a few times, that whole
process. And eventually, we found that antisemitic content was being served to those
minors.
We conducted a random 90-minute process of manual training, and then we filtered
for relevance, collected all those accounts and then we built a bespoke bot to
continue watching those accounts, based on the indicators that we provided, and we
ended up with a large dataset of videos which we transcribed to understand the
volume of antisemitic content that was being served to minors. And what we found,
it was within that 90-minute training session, a young 15 year old boy - so
a minor - was served content glorifying the IRGC, Holocaust-denial content and
antisemitic conspiracy theories.

MR BESHARA: You mention in your report that AI is changing both the nature of
antisemitic content online and exacerbating its spread. Can you elaborate briefly on
the role of AI, both in moderating through use of LLMs and other AI systems, the
content on the platforms, but also as a driver of antisemitism online through
AI-generated images and visuals and then -

MS ROSE: Yes. So online antisemitism is often highly aestheticised. By that I mean
that it's not just delivered through a set of messages, but through memes, images,
inferred meaning, and that creates effectively an aesthetic culture which is
particularly common in far right, but also we've evidenced it in digital Salafi
ecosystems where users feel empowered as part of that ecosystem based on the
visual aesthetics. And it's often united by that aesthetic, not necessarily by an
ideology, but significantly plays a role in the spread of antisemitism through memes
which use crude humour and desensitise users to violence and to antisemitism.
We've seen generative AI used by harmful actors to promote antisemitism in
a number of ways. I should say that images have been used since long before
generative AIs. So I wouldn't want to overstate the fact that this - I wouldn't want to
say that this has come around in the last few years, but what that has done is made it
more accessible to users who wouldn't otherwise be able to make highly viral
content.
There's a couple of examples I draw upon in the report. The first is a piece of
research which we delivered a couple of years ago now, where we looked at the role
of generative AI in content about the Holocaust and tried to understand whether we
could create Holocaust denial content from a number of different models of
generative AI. In terms of Holocaust denial, that's sometimes a bit more difficult, and
there were a number of safeguards in place. But for distortive content, it was a lot
more of a complex picture.
We managed achieve creating images of children smiling in concentration camps, for
example, or playing outside the bunks of Auschwitz. That's particularly concerning,
because it's not overtly illegal in any sense, but it does erode that memory of
Holocaust and changes the narrative and means that the facts of the Holocaust are
brought into question. And so that is one form of harm coming from generative AI.
Another form which we identified recently as well was the use of generative AI to
recreate Hitler's speeches in English, which went viral and were viewed many times.
This is obviously a technology that wasn't previously available and means that Nazi
content is available to a wider user basis than just those who speak German. And we
found hostile states using generative AI in their content. So, for example, we found is
use of it from Iranian-linked accounts which is likely played a role in the ability of
that content to go viral. So the first point to make is around generative AI and the
way in which that has lowered the barrier to participation and production of viral
antisemitic content and increased the views, likely, on that content.
And AI is also used to produce recommender algorithms and train as algorithms, and
where either antisemitic content is identified, it's then pumped through those
recommender algorithms, and so to users who wouldn't otherwise see it and that
creates a false filter bubble where users believe that - users normalise those ideas
because those are the only ideas that they see.

We note here an example from the UK in 2024 where an individual who conducted
an attack, on a - motivated by violence fixation - an attack on a girls' dance class in
Southport. A false name of the attacker was spread online shortly after, where the
attacker was alleged to be Muslim and alleged to be an immigrant that had recently
arrived on a small boat crossing the Channel.
That was false and confirmed by the police to be false the next day. But still when
you typed Southport where the attack had taken place, into the search bar of TikTok,
the recommended algorithm served you the false name of the attacker. That went on
to play a significant role in what we tracked as the rise of anti-Muslim and
anti-migrant hate on social media and eventual widespread riots across the UK
against Muslin migrant communities. So here we can see that connectivity between
the all those different pieces of harm and platform structures that exacerbate the
issue.
And, finally, AI plays a role in automated content moderation by platforms
themselves and I can't speak exactly to what role that plays because that information
is not publicly available. But we know that platforms have indicated that they do use
automated moderation to detect and to remove antisemitic content.

possible regulatory responses that you have explored in your report. You have
mentioned the Digital Services Act and the UK Online Safety Act. Can you just
beginning perhaps with DSA, walk us through the key elements of the framework as
you see them and how they might be adapted for other jurisdictions?
MS ROSE: So some of the key, I guess, distinguishing features of the Digital
Services Act which are mentioned here, is the kind of dual reporting system both for
illegal content but also for content which violates the platform's terms of service.
And so you have a dual system where a user is required to actually have some, quite
some level of legal knowledge in order to flag a piece of content to the platform, and
then the platforms have a responsibility to respond to that content in a meaningful
way.
That flagging system is reasonably common across these kind of frameworks. One of
the key differences with the Digital Services Act, which we see, is the transparency
requirements where platforms are required to publish transparency reports and this is
really quite significant. This is the only regulatory framework where platforms are
systematically required to produce those reports. And so that gives us the best insight
we have into how these platforms are performing in terms of moderation and in
terms of those regulatory requirements.

They're not quite standardised, they're not quite comparable because of the structures
of those reports, and what's mandated by the DSA at the moment; but they're the top
standard for what's available globally around transparency.
MR BESHARA: And I understand there are other limitations associated with those

been removed. For example, removal - content that is removed will just be classified
under one category rather than separated out into, say, antisemitic content or
anti-Muslim content and so on. Is that another limitation of these reports?
MS ROSE: Yes, exactly. So different platforms will take different approaches.

number of reports received. So although they will say "We removed X number of
reports" we can't understand that in the context of how many overall pieces of
antisemitic content were available. Some other platforms take different approaches.
Meta aggregates hate speech under illegal content. So we don't even know what form
of content that is and then it's not disaggregated by a form of hate speech. So we
don't have publicly information available about the volume of antisemitism. It's not
placed into context around the overall volume. There's a number of other
transparency mechanisms that could be strengthened here.
One is around the number of human moderators in different languages, but also in
different country contexts. So platforms, for example, will indicate under one of X's
transparency reports that there's over 1,300 moderators in English but we don't know
where those moderators are located and so, for example, would they have the cultural
competence or knowledge of the Australian context or would they all be located in
the US and that's quite an important point when you think about the nuances and
specificities of local forms of hate.
Also, that's clear to us, for example, in this X report that I cite, that there's not
necessarily the combination of language and subject matter expertise. So Poland, in
this report, was found to have one language moderator for all violative content that's
not just illegal and it's not hate speech; and in this report Sweden had zero. So there's
quite a disparity across jurisdictions; and, of course, that will impact Australians who
speak multiple languages and have dual nationalities, for example.
We still don't have any insights on how moderators are trained; any systematic
insights on how decisions are made. We don't have any transparency of algorithmic
systems, and we don't have any comparability across different reports. So this is
a great start, this transparency regime, but it doesn't quite give us the information we
need in order to be able to make those decisions.
The other point that I would be really keen to make here would be around data access

comprehensive, and means that we don't have a picture of what is going on online. It

under-moderation and over-moderation and this is a vital point for ensuring that free
speech and democratic integrity is maintained in the online space from both
perspectives as well.

platforms?

additional transparency that we're able to garner from systems such as the Oversight
